evidence_quotes.quote: We obtained estimates of the percentage of national populations with access to improved sanitation and water – for various years between 2000 and 2012 – from the 2013 Country Files of the Joint Monitoring Programme for Water Supply and Sanitation

In regression analyses, we investigated associations between the normalized rates of change in population access and national socioeconomic indicators: gross national income per capita, government effectiveness, official development assistance, freshwater resources, education, poverty, Gini coefficient, child mortality and the human development index.
In future studies, the effect on progress of additional variables that assess the enabling environment and governance should be investigated.
The normalized rates of change indicated that most of the investigated countries were making progress towards achieving universal access to improved drinking water and sanitation.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines national population access to improved drinking water and improved sanitation (including shared toilet facilities) across 73 countries between 2000 and 2012 using household survey data compiled by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme.
criterion_notes.c2: PLAIN WORDING: Passes ('yes') because one of the nine national independent variables tested in PCA and regression models is 'government effectiveness' from the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (a composite macro-governance performance metric). NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING: Fails ('no') because the study examines nine broad national socioeconomic, resource, aid, and composite macro-governance indicators (GNI per capita, WGI government effectiveness, per-capita WASH official development assistance, freshwater resources per capita, female secondary education, extreme poverty, Gini coefficient, under-5 mortality, and HDI) rather than any rule-type legal, administrative, institutional, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement/disconnection, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). GLAAS policy/budget variables were explicitly excluded from analysis, and the authors note that governance and enabling-environment variables remain for future studies. Note: exclusion is strictly on exposure scope grounds, not on the null statistical findings.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical quantitative cross-national study using JMP household survey series (at least 5 data points across at least 3 years per country), frontier efficiency normalization in R, principal components analysis, and univariate/multivariate linear and fractional logistic regressions in Stata.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports baseline year-2000 coverage (%), absolute linear rates of change (%/year), and frontier-normalized rates of change (-1 to 1) in national population access to improved drinking water (n = 67 countries) and improved sanitation (n = 61 countries).
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis and sample (country-level panel/cross-section of 73 countries: 67 for drinking water, 61 for sanitation, derived from nationally representative household surveys), exposures (nine national socioeconomic and macro-governance indicators), outcomes (absolute and normalized rates of change in water and sanitation coverage), and study design (cross-national ecological frontier and regression analysis) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with abstracts also provided in Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian, and Spanish).

study_design: Cross-national ecological longitudinal and regression study using non-parametric frontier efficiency normalization, principal components analysis, and linear and fractional logistic regressions
country: 73 countries (multi-country cross-national analysis; mainly low- and middle-income countries)
population_and_sample: National populations of 73 countries (n = 67 countries for drinking water; n = 61 countries for sanitation) with at least five nationally representative household survey/census data points spanning at least three years between 2000 and 2012 in WHO/UNICEF JMP Country Files; unit of analysis is the country
exposure: Nine national socioeconomic and macro-governance indicators (year 2000 or closest available): GNI per capita, World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators government effectiveness, per-capita official development assistance for water and sanitation, renewable internal freshwater resources per capita, female secondary education completion (>25 years), poverty (<US$1.25/day), Gini coefficient, under-5 mortality rate, and Human Development Index (plus top three PCA synthetic components)
outcome: Absolute linear rate of change (%/year) and frontier-normalized rate of change (-1 to 1) in national population access to improved drinking water and improved sanitation (including shared facilities) over 2000–2012
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically analyses cross-national progress in household drinking water and sanitation access across 73 countries (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6) and includes a broad composite macro-governance index (World Bank WGI 'government effectiveness') alongside eight socioeconomic/aid/resource indicators (which would qualify under the literal plain wording of Criterion 2), it does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or institutional mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, administrative burden, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Eligibility is assessed strictly on exposure scope, independent of the null regression results.
